extracted.intended_audience: copyright scholars, policymakers, Copyright Office officials, and intellectual property practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and comparative analysis for creating an administrative small-claims process for copyright infringement (design choices, limits, remedies, and procedural features). Intended to inform policy design and evaluation of forum alternatives to federal district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites to bring a federal copyright infringement claim
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a federal claim for copyright infringement, the owner first must prove that she is the registered owner of the material; the work must be original, exhibit a modicum of creativity, and be within the subject matter of copyright; the plaintiff must show the defendant wrongfully exercised one or more of the six exclusive rights granted under the Copyright Act; upon filing a complaint the plaintiff bears the burden of proving a prima facie case of infringement, and the defendant can present affirmative defenses (e.g., fair use, copyright misuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 17 U.S.C. § 411 and related authorities; note that complex affirmative defenses and the statutory framework shape which forums can adequately adjudicate disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration requirement and foreign-author exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copyright Act generally requires registration before bringing a U.S. federal infringement claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign authors are exempted from the registration requirement under the Berne Convention (art. 18). See 17 U.S.C. § 411 and Berne Convention discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing as gate for administrative track
rubrics_metrics.description: An online administrative submission process would require a prima facie showing of infringement for a case to proceed before an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) in the Copyright Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a prima facie case encourages straightforward, easy cases to self-select into the administrative track and reduces frivolous or factually complex matters in the administrative forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies in an administrative proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies available could include monetary damages currently available under the copyright statute and could be expanded to include remedies such as enforcing licenses, requiring attribution, and designating frequent, willful copyright infringers as 'repeat offenders' to notify ISPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designing new remedies (e.g., ISP notifications) could increase deterrence and interact with DMCA safe-harbor rules (17 U.S.C. § 512).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: inability to seek injunctive relief administratively
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative proceeding would likely not permit seeking injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a significant disadvantage compared to federal court, where injunctive relief is available; proponents of federal small claims courts highlight the value of preserving injunctive remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty adjudicating affirmative defenses (e.g., fair use) in an administrative forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative proceedings may face challenges in hearing and resolving affirmative defenses such as fair use; some defenses might be passed on or dismissed without prejudice and handled in regular courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex factual disputes may be inappropriate for an expedited administrative track; parties may need a path to district court for full adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined online process benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: An online forum reduces travel needs, lowers the likelihood that an attorney is required, is simpler and more efficient than filing a complaint in federal district court, and would improve access to remedies for more copyright owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected benefits include faster resolution, lower costs, and reduced federal-court docket pressure; encourages public participation and respects copyright law by increasing enforceability for small owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited discovery and no in-person hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals (e.g., Lemley–Reese) envisage online proceedings with no in-person hearings and limited discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited discovery saves time and money but may impede resolving disputes that require factual development; appropriate for straightforward cases but not for complex factual disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals structure and discouragement of frivolous appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial decisions could be appealed to a panel of ALJs, with a further option to take disputes to district court; courts could discourage fruitless appeals by making losing appellants pay costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeals ladder preserves access to courts while discouraging meritless appeals; the balance affects finality and deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-infringement threshold for administrative eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested eligibility filter is requiring a minimum number of infringements (e.g., fifty uploads during any thirty-day period) for bringing certain types of claims (such as p2p network cases) in the administrative forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds help target administrative resources to repeat or large-scale infringers and reduce trivial or isolated disputes entering the admin track.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADR (mediation/arbitration–mediation) suitability and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation or a mixed arbitration–mediation program can resolve many IP disputes using limited discovery and experienced neutrals; arbitration–mediation can produce a sealed decision that encourages settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADR reduces costs and preserves confidentiality but is voluntary and thus less useful for plaintiffs seeking statutory damages or for parties unwilling to settle; ADR still requires filing a complaint and thus may burden resource-poor claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal small claims court model features
rubrics_metrics.description: A specialized federal small claims court could offer an 'expedited and simplistic' process using ALJs, relaxed rules of evidence and procedure, and could be a mandatory first step before district court; it could hear affirmative defenses and injunctive relief and allow parties to agree to make the proceeding nonbinding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model preserves more of the substantive remedies available in federal court (including injunctions) and provides dedicated judges knowledgeable in IP, but discovery costs and federal docket burdens may remain; logistics include where to locate such courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate over caps on damages in small-claims forums
rubrics_metrics.description: There is tension over whether to impose jurisdictional damage caps in a small-claims forum: concerns arise because statutory damages for copyright can range from $750 to $30,000 per infringement, making a blanket cap controversial; alternative proposals (for patents) suggest ceilings (e.g., $1 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps affect access to remedies, potential fairness, and alignment with statutory damage regimes; any cap design must consider statutory structure and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents County Court (PCC) and UK small-claims features as analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCC model includes two-day trials, careful control of cross-examination, no formal cap on damages (but recommendation to send very large cases to High Court), time limits on written evidence, and ability for non-attorneys to represent parties; ADR is encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural limits produce faster, lower-cost proceedings and can inform U.S. small-claims design, but translations must account for differences in remedies and legal culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: TTAB limitations and Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR)
rubrics_metrics.description: TTAB proceedings are limited to determining registration or cancellation and cannot award damages or injunctions; TTAB's ACR addresses smaller, less complicated cases by requiring parties to stipulate that the TTAB can resolve disputed facts on a written record, delivering faster decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TTAB/ACR shows how administrative adjudication can be expedited for limited-remedy disputes if parties accept written-record adjudication and narrower relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs, discovery burdens, and access-to-justice tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: High litigation costs and discovery burdens in federal court deter plaintiffs (especially small copyright owners) and may lead to inequitable settlements; streamlined/administrative/ADR processes reduce costs but have other limits (e.g., limited remedies, voluntariness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of any small-claims forum must balance reduced procedural costs against fair adjudication and substantive remedy availability to avoid unfair pressure on small parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation via notice-and-comment to support reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment processes can lay bare the intricacies of copyright law for the public, encourage public input, and help build momentum for statutory or administrative reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engaging the public may increase legitimacy and reveal practical concerns from diverse stakeholder groups (e.g., photographers, writers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum location and logistical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions must be made whether to locate a federal small-claims court in each federal district or only in a few districts near major IP centers (e.g., New York, Nashville, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location choices affect access (travel costs), workload distribution, and administrative feasibility; online submission models mitigate some location concerns.
